 Religious holidays bill vetoed by Lombardo could become law in Nevada's next session
 Assemblymember Reuben D’Silva, a Las Vegas Democrat and Purple Heart recipient, is one of just two members of the Nevada Legislature who has served in the U.S. military. Photo by:
 Steve Marcus 
 By
 Ava Chatlosh 
 ( contact )
 Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026 | 2 a.m.
 Editor's note: Este artículo está traducido al español. 
 Nevada Assemblymember Reuben D’Silva, D-Las Vegas, wants Diwali, Eid al-Fitr, Vaisakhi and Vesak on the state calendar.
 A veto stopped his first attempt, but this time he says Gov.-elect Aaron Ford has promised to sign it.
 D’Silva reintroduced legislation last week that would make the four holidays days of observance in Nevada. The Hindu, Muslim, Sikh and Buddhist holidays carry cultural importance similar to what Easter or Christmas hold for Christians, he said.
 If the bill passes, Nevada would become the fourth state to recognize Diwali, the third to recognize Eid and the first to recognize Vaisakhi and Vesak.
 Assembly Bill 82 had broad bipartisan support during the 2025 session, passing 33-9 in the Assembly and 15-6 in the state Senate, before Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo vetoed it. It was one of a state-record 87 bills vetoed during the 2025 session.
 “The official reason was that there were too many holidays on the list of days of observance,” D’Silva said.
 Lombardo also vetoed other cultural observance measures and asked their sponsors to apply for a proclamation instead. He did sign one bill designating a day of observance: Senate Bill 96 designating Jan. 27 as “International Holocaust Remembrance Day” in Nevada .
 D’Silva said he had expected Lombardo to sign the holiday legislation.
 “I really think that it was a campaign move, because there was such a backlash against diversity initiatives,” D’Silva said.
 D’Silva said he is also reintroducing a reparations study bill. His 2025 version would have created a Juneteenth commission and tasked a legislative subcommittee with studying racial discrimination in Nevada — including potential forms of restitution or rehabilitation for descendants — before Lombardo vetoed it.
 According to D’Silva, both bills have the support of Ford, a Democrat who unseated Lombardo earlier this month and will take office in 2027.
 Democrats have voting control of both houses of the state Legislature, meaning many of the bills vetoed by Lombardo could be introduced and signed into law by Ford. Ford has said he would sign several within his first 30 days, including a bill capping prescription drug prices at Medicare levels, universal free school meals and limits on corporate homebuying.
 “Gov.-elect Ford gave me strong assurance that he’s going to sign both of those as long as I can work them through the Legislature and get them to his desk,” D’Silva said.
 D’Silva emphasized that these holidays are not like other national days, such as “National Hot Dog Day.” They have been celebrated for thousands of years by millions of people.
 “These are a deep part of a human story; these are celebrations of fate and culture,” D’Silva said.
 D’Silva, who is Catholic, pointed to India, where Christians make up 2% of the population and Christmas is an official federal holiday. That kind of recognition matters because it makes people feel included, he said.
 “It’s about visibility and representation, and being incorporated into the broader society,” D’Silva said.
 Diwali, a major festival of lights celebrated by more than a billion people, is recognized by California, Pennsylvania and Connecticut. Eid, a Muslim celebration of the breaking of the fast that marks the end of Ramadan, is recognized by California and Washington.
 The legislation is one of 93 bills Nevada legislators have introduced so far. Although the session doesn’t begin until February, incumbents can introduce bills for the next session as soon as the last one ends.
 D’Silva said recognition of these holidays has come up again and again in his community. Even if it doesn’t cost any money or make any tangible change, he said, it is important to his constituents.
 Constituents tell him, "'We never had anybody who represented us, who could understand the community,'” D’Silva said. “It may sound basic to other folks, but having our religious holidays observed on the Nevada calendar is a huge deal when it comes to being accepted.”
